title: Everyday Greetings
introduction: Greet someone in the morning, afternoon or evening, and end a chat politely.
summary: You practised greetings through the day and a see-you-later farewell.

exercises.prompt: You meet a neighbour at breakfast time. Choose the morning greeting that asks how they slept.
exercises.explanation: Ina kwana? is a morning greeting asking how someone slept.

exercises.prompt: You arrive to visit a friend in the afternoon. Which greeting asks about their day?
exercises.explanation: Ina wuni? is used as an afternoon greeting, asking about the day.

exercises.prompt: You meet a friend in the evening and are staying to chat. Choose a good-evening greeting.
exercises.explanation: Barka da yamma is a good-evening expression.

exercises.prompt: Your friendly chat is over and you will see each other later. What do you say as you leave?
exercises.explanation: Sai an jima means see you later. It is a parting expression.

title: Introduce Yourself
introduction: Share your name, ask a new acquaintance their name and say where you are from.
summary: You practised sharing your name, addressing name questions to a man or woman and saying where you are from.

exercises.prompt: You join a community group. Your name is Amina. Choose your introduction.
exercises.explanation: Sunana ... means my name is ... Here the name is Amina.

exercises.prompt: A man has introduced himself only with a greeting. Which question asks his name?
exercises.explanation: Mi sunanka? asks a man what his name is. The ending changes with the person addressed.

exercises.prompt: A woman has greeted you but has not said her name. Which question asks her name?
exercises.explanation: Mi sunanki? asks a woman what her name is.

exercises.prompt: You are from Kano and a new acquaintance asks where you are from. Choose the matching statement.
exercises.explanation: Na fito daga ... means I am from ... Here the place is Kano.

title: Family & People
introduction: Check in about someone’s family and understand questions about children or a spouse.
summary: You practised checking in about family, children, a husband and a wife.

exercises.prompt: After greeting a friend, you want to ask how their family is. Which question fits?
exercises.explanation: Ina iyali? asks how your family is. It extends a friendly greeting.

exercises.prompt: A friend asks “Ina yara?” Your children are doing very well. Which reply fits?
exercises.explanation: Ina yara? asks how the children are. Lafiya lau gives a positive reply: very well.

exercises.prompt: Your friend has mentioned their husband. You would like to ask how he is. Which question fits?
exercises.explanation: Ina miji? asks how your husband is.

exercises.prompt: Your friend has mentioned their wife. You would like to ask how she is. Which question fits?
exercises.explanation: Ina mata? asks how your wife is.

title: Food & Drink
introduction: At a shared meal, say you are hungry, express a food preference and recognise an offered drink.
summary: You practised expressing hunger, wanting pineapple, declining chicken and recognising water.

exercises.prompt: You have not eaten yet and your host asks how you feel. Choose the statement that says you are hungry.
exercises.explanation: Ina jin yunwa means I feel hungry.

exercises.prompt: Your host offers a choice of fruit. You would like pineapple. Which statement fits?
exercises.explanation: Ina son abarba can mean I like or want pineapple. In this situation, you are choosing pineapple.

exercises.prompt: A friend is choosing food for a shared meal. You do not like chicken. Which statement tells them that preference?
exercises.explanation: Ba na son kaza means I do not like chicken.

exercises.prompt: After a warm walk, your host offers “ruwa.” What are they offering you?
exercises.explanation: Ruwa is water. This is an offer of a drink.
